messages.subject: Tidal currents and distance sampling
parts:
Dear all,

I am currently planning boat based surveys in support of the EIA process for
a tidal energy device, and I'm beginning to think about the interpretation
of the data. I can see that strong tidal currents might have important
consequences for both the accuracy of density estimates (e.g. with a tidal
current perpendicular to the transect additional birds "flowing" into the
transect from the side) and their interpretation (e.g. birds/m2 or
birds/m2/second) and that these consequences will depend critically upon
whether birds are holding their position against the current, or flowing
with it, or some position in between.



Is this a problem other people have encountered or are encountering, and
there is guidance available on how deal with this situation, including what
needs recording in the field (e.g. water speed as well as ground speed).



Any guidance gratefully received.



Many thanks



Nigel Harding

messages.author: 6e15de0134e98c08
messages.subject: Re: Tidal currents and distance sampling
parts:
Dear Nigel, list,

Your study seems quite interesting, but I'm not sure you provide all the=20
required information to answer the questions you ask. The best way to=20
address the problem will depend strongly on what are the purposes of=20
inference, namely at what spatial and temporal scale do you require=20
density estimates, as well as how serious/persistent the tidal currents a=
re.

From the distance sampling perspective, if what you have is a line=20
transect and the tidal current is perpendicular to it, one of the=20
fundamental conventional distance sampling assumptions is violated: you=20
have non-random movement, as animals are coming towards you; if their=20
speed is negligible to boat speed, you might ignore it, but otherwise=20
you run into trouble and will tend to overestimate abundance. In that=20
sense, it might better to attempt to have the transect parallel to the=20
current, but then other issues might pop up (e.g. if there's some animal=20
density gradient with respect to the lines).

I hope this helps.

Cheers,

Tiago
